numeric.description: ISO 3166-1 numeric code, zero-padded; null if none (e.g. Kosovo)

system.description: Human-readable description of the system of government

systemType.description: How power is held in practice. absolute-monarchy (shown on the page as "Ruling monarchy"): a monarch who rules as well as reigns, with or without a constitution and an elected chamber (Saudi Arabia, Oman, Jordan, Morocco, Brunei, Monaco, Liechtenstein). parliamentary-monarchy (shown as "Constitutional monarchy"): a monarch who reigns while the head of government governs. The rule between them: a monarchy is a ruling monarchy where executive.leader names its monarch (headOfState) or regent, and a parliamentary-monarchy where it names the head of government; the one exception is Saudi Arabia, a ruling monarchy whose crown prince governs as prime minister. one-party: one party rules and others are banned or subordinate. theocratic: religious authority holds supreme power (the Holy See, Iran). military: the armed forces hold power after a coup, including juntas that call themselves transitional. transitional: a civilian interim arrangement on the way to a new constitution or election. dependent-territory: self-governing but not sovereign (Greenland).

status.description: in-flux = government formation, caretaker, disputed or election under way

leader.description: Which of them holds the most power in practice: the person the map names for the country. regent: where a regent exercises the head of state's powers on his behalf while he stays head of state (Liechtenstein, where Hereditary Prince Alois has acted for Prince Hans-Adam II since 15 August 2004); the regent is then recorded in executive.regent, which this value requires. headOfGovernment in parliamentary systems, where the prime minister or chancellor governs and the monarch or president is mostly ceremonial. headOfState where the president, monarch or party leader directs the government: presidential systems; presidents who dominate their governments (France, Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, Azerbaijan, Moldova); one-party states whose party leader is head of state (China, Cuba); ruling monarchs, emirs and sultans (Monaco, Qatar, Oman) and the Pope; a supreme leader above the elected president (Iran); the head of a military government. Where a crown prince or premier who is not head of state governs, as in Saudi Arabia, it is headOfGovernment. Judge by practice, not by the constitution's wording alone, and say why in reviewNote when it changes.

regent.description: Only where someone exercises the head of state's powers on his behalf (a regent or permanent deputy), who stays head of state. Record it with executive.leader "regent" when the regent holds the most power in practice.
